title: Benign prostate enlargement: urinary symptoms and treatment choices
intro: Benign prostate enlargement is non-cancerous growth of the prostate, a gland below the bladder. Enlargement can affect urine flow, but not every urinary symptom comes from the prostate. Symptoms may include a weak stream, difficulty starting, urgency or waking at night to urinate. Assessment helps distinguish bothersome but manageable symptoms from infection, retention or another condition requiring different care.

sections.heading: Explain the effect on daily life
paragraphs: Tell the clinician about the stream, frequency, leakage, discomfort and whether the bladder feels incompletely emptied. Explain disturbed sleep, restrictions at work or worry about finding toilets. A diary of drinks and urination may help if requested. Prostate size does not tell the whole story about symptoms. Medicines and other health problems can contribute, so bring a complete list, including non-prescription cold remedies and supplements. Do not stop prescribed medicines on your own.

sections.heading: Understand the examination and tests
paragraphs: Assessment may include an examination, urine testing and selected blood tests. A specialist may measure urine flow or how much remains in the bladder. Discuss the purpose and limitations of a PSA blood test if it is offered: an increased value is not by itself a cancer diagnosis. Benign enlargement is not the same as prostate cancer, but the conditions can coexist. New urinary symptoms still deserve assessment rather than reassurance based only on age.

sections.heading: Match the plan to symptoms and priorities
paragraphs: Mild symptoms without complications may be monitored with advice rather than treated immediately. Discuss the timing of drinks, caffeine or alcohol if relevant, while maintaining appropriate hydration and following any individual fluid advice. Do not respond by severely restricting fluids. Bladder habits or other practical changes should fit the cause of symptoms. Agree how to judge progress and when to review the plan, especially if sleep or daily functioning remains affected.

sections.heading: Compare medicines and procedures realistically
paragraphs: Some medicines relax muscles around the outlet; others act on prostate growth or particular bladder symptoms. Benefits, speed of effect and side effects differ, including possible dizziness or sexual effects. Procedures may be considered for persistent troublesome symptoms or complications. Ask about bleeding, recovery, continence, ejaculation and the possibility of needing further treatment, according to the proposed procedure. A treatment chosen for someone else is not automatically the right choice for you.

sections.heading: Know the signs that should not wait
paragraphs: New inability to pass urine needs urgent medical help, particularly with a full or painful bladder. A catheter may be needed to drain it; do not wait for a routine appointment or try to force the problem away with large drinks. Blood in urine, painful urination, fever or flank pain also need prompt advice. Severe illness, confusion or collapse requires emergency help. If symptoms change after treatment, seek reassessment rather than assuming all changes are expected ageing.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: preparing a useful review
examples.text: Someone wakes repeatedly to urinate and worries about taking long journeys. They describe the effect on sleep and bring their medicine list and requested diary. They ask whether the prostate, bladder or another condition explains the symptoms, instead of buying a product marketed for prostate health.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: recognising retention
examples.text: A person with a previously weak stream suddenly cannot urinate and feels increasing bladder discomfort. They seek urgent help rather than waiting for their next prescription review. They explain when they last passed urine and any recent medicines or other symptoms.

questions: What is the likely cause of my symptoms, and what do the proposed tests add?
Which monitoring, medicine or procedure options fit my priorities and risk of complications?
What side effects and warning signs matter, and when should we review the plan?
